item.title: The Daily Star – The dangers of a fragmented health system in Bangladesh
item.description:
The government that took office in February inherits a health sector that almost everyone agrees is in a fragile state. Public health spending sits below one percent of GDP, among the lowest shares in South Asia, while households pay roughly 70 percent of all health costs directly, one of the highest out-of-pocket burdens in the world. On top of this came a donor shock: the 2025 suspension of USAID-funded programmes, which hollowed out tuberculosis control, research and frontline services almost overnight. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s administration has made healthcare reform a stated pillar of its agenda, promising stronger primary care and wider access to affordable healthcare. It will not get far if, at the same time, the state quietly dismantles the one planning architecture that delivered most of the gains the country still boasts about.

That dismantling is already under way. In early 2025, the Planning Commission concluded that the proposed Fifth Health, Population and Nutrition Sector Programme, worth roughly Tk 1 lakh crore (about US$8.6 billion) across 38 operational plans for 2025 to 2029, should not run as a sector programme at all. Most of it, the commission reasoned, falls within the ministry’s core responsibilities and belongs in the ordinary revenue budget rather than under a project-style umbrella. The fifth HPNSP is now being treated as a sector action plan with an exit plan. After twenty-seven years, the sector-wide approach (SWAp) is being allowed to lapse. That would be a mistake, not because the SWAp was perfect, but because the alternative on offer is precisely the fragmentation the SWAp was designed to address.

It is worth remembering why Bangladesh adopted this model in the first place. Throughout the 1980s and early 1990s, health and family planning were financed through a range of separate government- and donor-supported projects, an arrangement that was, in the government’s own later assessment, neither efficient nor sustainable. The Health and Population Sector Strategy of 1997 marked a deliberate break. From the first Health and Population Sector Programme of 1998 onwards, the ministry adopted a single sector plan, funded jointly by the government and development partners through pooled and parallel financing, implemented through operational plans and reviewed every year by independent teams against agreed indicators.
Patients and their relatives crowd the outpatient department of Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital in Dhaka in June 2025, waiting their turn at the ticket counters for treatment they can afford. Households pay roughly 70 percent of all health costs directly, one of the highest out-of-pocket burdens in the world. Photo: Prabir Das

The results, documented in a 2016 assessment of fifteen years of the SWAp in Health Policy and Planning, are not a matter of nostalgia. The approach aligned funding and technical support with national priorities, put the ministry rather than the donors in charge of designing and reviewing the programme, and built lasting institutions for procurement, financial management and monitoring. It also changed how the ministry worked. A single joint annual review replaced the previous multitude of separate donor missions, each aligned with a different financial year, sparing staff the time once lost to preparing for one visitor after another; demanding as it was every spring, that one review brought the development partners on board and, through close monitoring, improved both fund utilisation and operational plan performance. A pared-down common set of indicators replaced the project-by-project reporting that individual donors had previously required, and the management information systems strengthened in those years remain an asset that would outlast any single programme. 

Over the SWAp years, the contraceptive prevalence rate climbed past 60 percent, the use of modern methods rose by roughly 30 percent across the period, immunisation coverage remained above 90 percent, and the maternal mortality ratio fell sharply. This was the era when Bangladesh became a global health success story, and the gains, as public health experts now recall, rested on exactly what a SWAp institutionalises: coordinated national programmes backed by a strong partnership between the government, donors and non-governmental providers. Sustained immunisation coverage above 90 percent remains living proof that a coordinated national programme can succeed even within a constrained system.

Then progress stalled, and how it stalled is the real warning. After falling by about 40 percent between 2001 and 2010, from 322 to 194 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births, the maternal mortality ratio barely moved over the following six years, standing at 196 in 2016, even as skilled birth attendance nearly doubled and facility deliveries continued to increase. The gains in coverage had simply stopped translating into lives saved. In the first decade, having a skilled attendant at birth measurably lowered a mother’s risk of dying; in the second, it no longer did, because deliveries had shifted to public and private facilities that were not equipped to manage obstetric emergencies. Emerging risks, such as repeat births among teenage mothers, went untracked, while the programme continued to deploy interventions designed for an earlier phase. Bangladesh, as one widely shared verdict puts it, harvested the low-hanging fruit of prevention but failed to develop the capacity to undertake the harder work of building a mature health system.

That was a failure of stewardship as much as of resources, and the SWAp was meant to address it. The whole point of a sector programme is that it is a learning system: each annual review is supposed to assess what is working and refine the following year’s interventions based on the evidence. That discipline lapsed, though not for lack of evidence. The ministry’s own joint annual programme reviews and policy briefs highlighted the same weaknesses in successive cycles, from the unfinished integration of services to the neglect of quality and readiness. The findings were acknowledged and then set aside as the government repeatedly resorted to incremental, copy-pasted budgets and large infrastructure projects.

Worse, under the previous government, the health budget came to be treated in important respects as a source of rents rather than results. The interim administration’s own White Paper on the economy documented systematic corruption running through health-sector procurement, supply chains and appointments, and subsequent procurement audits found that a large share of the health directorate’s contracts went to single bidders, with equipment sometimes left unused until it deteriorated. Transparency International Bangladesh, in successive national household surveys between 2018 and 2024, repeatedly identified public healthcare as one of the country’s most corruption-affected service sectors. A budget steered towards extraction cannot also be steered by evidence. Restarting the SWAp means restoring the very function it was designed to serve: the annual, evidence-based refinement of what the sector actually does.

The deeper diagnosis, on which independent analysts now broadly agree, is fragmentation. The Universal Health Care (UHC) Forum describes a sector hobbled by fragmented service delivery and weak referral systems, and warns that UHC is unattainable without reforming the existing system. A leading health economist points to a complex, multi-layered institutional structure spanning multiple ministries and agencies as a major source of implementation bottlenecks (Syed Abdul Hamid, The Business Standard, 29 January 2026). Another argues bluntly that the country must abandon its incremental, copy-paste budgeting and pursue interconnected structural reforms instead. The previous government, far from addressing this fragmentation, deepened it. It never resolved the decades-old separation between the health services and family planning wings that every sector programme since 1998 was meant to integrate, and in 2017 it split the ministry itself into two divisions, each under its own secretary. A government commission has since found that the split brought no improvements, instead widening the coordination gap and duplicating work, which is why the present government is now moving to reunite the two divisions.
A nurse administers oral polio vaccine drops to a baby at Sramajibi Hospital during an immunisation campaign. Sustained immunisation coverage remains a testament to the success of Bangladesh’s coordinated national health programmes. Photo: Star

There was a related shift in spending priorities. In its later years, the sector programme leaned increasingly towards visible infrastructure, such as new buildings and equipment, and away from the unglamorous work of strengthening systems that actually improves outcomes, such as supervision, referral, supply chains, workforce development and quality of care. This is why the country has an extensive network of health facilities that nonetheless remains trapped in low productivity, and why experts now urge the government to invest in primary care rather than in more hospitals. Pushing health spending back into scattered revenue budget lines runs in exactly the wrong direction. It removes the one mechanism that required the ministry, the Finance Division and external partners to sit at a single table, agree on priorities and account for their progress once a year. Strip that away and Bangladesh does not get a leaner system. It returns to the pre-1998 world.

None of this is an argument that the SWAp should return unchanged. The same evidence base is candid about its failures, and any honest case for its revival must be too. The Bangladeshi version was always a hybrid: it financed an agreed portion of the ministry’s activities while allowing large off-budget projects and expensive infrastructure investments to proceed outside it, quietly diverting resources and weakening accountability. Planning was overcentralised. And for all the headline gains, equity lagged, as the gap between rich and poor in skilled birth attendance and other essential services widened rather than narrowed. Critics are also right that money already allocated often goes unspent and that buildings and equipment sit idle. But these are indictments of weak stewardship and poor absorptive capacity, not of the idea of governing the sector as a whole. 

As several experts stress, money alone is not the cure; higher budgets fail to deliver results unless resources are deployed by a capable workforce through transparent, accountable systems. A reformed SWAp is valuable precisely because it provides a framework for accountability, comprising an agreed plan and an independent annual review, which an individual revenue budget line does not.

The timing makes abandonment riskier still. The USAID withdrawal showed how dangerous it is to allow critical programmes to depend on uncoordinated external funding. In Dhaka, up to 40 percent of residents in informal settlements still depend on NGO- and donor-funded services for basic care, an arrangement experts describe as unsustainable. As aid grows scarcer and more conditional, a pooled, government-led financing platform that can absorb shocks and reallocate resources in line with agreed priorities is more valuable, not less.
Vacant beds at Moheshpur Upazila Health Complex in Jhenaidah. Despite Bangladesh’s extensive network of healthcare facilities, staff shortages and weak institutional capacity continue to undermine rural healthcare delivery. Photo: Star

It is also the natural vehicle for the government’s own ambitions. The state minister for health says the reform priorities now under discussion are largely identical to those in the ruling party’s manifesto and that a special cell has been formed to implement the manifesto’s commitments, alongside plans for an e-health card and one lakh new primary healthcare workers. The prime minister’s own advisers speak of a primary healthcare unit in every rural union and urban ward, a hundred thousand new recruits, and public health spending rising gradually towards 5 percent of GDP. Experts are pressing the government to adopt the Health Sector Reform Commission’s recommendations rather than shelve them as a relic of the interim government. Add the draft Universal Health Coverage Roadmap 2026–2035 and the National Health Compact signed in Tokyo last December, and the pattern is unmistakable. These are sector-wide ambitions. They cannot be delivered through a procurement line in someone’s annual budget.

So, the task before the new government is not to choose between retaining the old SWAp and abolishing it. It is to rebuild a more effective one. A restarted sector-wide approach should retain what worked, namely a single negotiated plan, pooled financing, independent annual reviews and ministry ownership, and address what did not. That means strengthening the ministry’s stewardship and regulatory functions, including separating its role as regulator from its role as service provider so that public and private facilities are subject to the same standards. It means closing the loopholes in the hybrid model so that off-budget projects and large-scale construction projects are brought within the plan and accounted for. It means integrating the fragmented primary healthcare network, comprising union sub-centres, family welfare centres and community clinics, under unified governance, and filling field-level vacancies that leave nearly a third of sanctioned health posts empty. It means devolving planning beyond Dhaka, extending coverage to urban and non-state healthcare services that the old programme ignored, and incorporating equity into the targets themselves.

The continuity of this approach across successive governments was once Bangladesh’s quiet advantage. A new administration with a clear mandate has a rare opportunity to build on that legacy and improve it. Letting the SWAp die by administrative default, without a replacement that can fulfil the same functions, is not reform. It is forgetting why the system was built.

Karar Zunaid Ahsan (email: [email protected]) teaches public health and programme evaluation at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill in the United States and previously worked on the management and monitoring of Bangladesh’s health SWAp. Md. Shamim Hayder Talukder has engaged with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare on behalf of civil society for the past 20 years. Peter Kim Streatfield is an emeritus scientist who has worked on Bangladesh’s health SWAp since its inception in 1997.

item.title: The Daily Star – Why we love imagining the history that never happened?
item.description:
Regime Change, Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan’s account of the first year of Donald Trump’s historically unprecedented return to the United States presidency, begins with an intriguing detour. For several pages, the authors imagine an alternative history in which Trump won re-election in 2020 and commenced his second term in 2021 rather than 2025.

In this scenario, Trump emerges from his first administration more cautious and constrained, lacking the opportunity to galvanise supporters through claims of electoral theft and political persecution. As a result, the upheavals that characterised his eventual return to office never occur. Had the 2020 election produced a different result, Haberman and Swan speculate, we might now be living in a calmer and more predictable world.

This desire to consider alternative histories, how the world might have changed if a known event had a different outcome, is shared by novelists and historians. Yet they generally pursue different aims.

All approaches to alternative history begin with what writers and scholars often describe as a point of divergence: a plausible change to recorded events that could have created a different timeline.

The possibilities are almost endless. What if Adolf Hitler had been assassinated in 1943 rather than dying by suicide in 1945? What if the Soviet Union had reached the Moon before the US in 1969? What if smallpox had never devastated the Indigenous peoples of North America? What if Christopher Columbus had failed to reach the Americas in 1492, only for European societies to face an Incan invasion decades later?

From a single altered event, entirely different worlds may emerge.

Fictional alternatives

Alternative history fiction is built upon this premise. This subgenre can be identified in literature as early as 1490. The chivalric romance Tirant lo Blanc tells the story of a wandering knight who manages to prevent the fall of Constantinople and the destruction of the Byzantine Empire.

But alternative histories really take off in the 19th and 20th centuries. Authors were drawn to imagine the unfamiliar realities that might have resulted from, for example, Napoleon’s successful conquest of Europe, or a Confederate victory in the American Civil War.

The history of the second world war, in particular, frequently invites this kind of speculation. Philip K. Dick’s classic The Man in the High Castle describes a US partitioned between Nazi Germany and Imperial Japan after the Axis powers triumph.
 
Cover of Philip K. Dick’s The Man in the High Castle (Gollancz, SF Masterworks edition; originally published in 1962).

Robert Harris’ Fatherland similarly depicts a post-war Nazi regime, using the conventions of noir crime fiction to reveal the hidden atrocities of the German state, 20 years after its victory.

More recently, New Zealand author Catherine Chidgey, in her novel The Book of Guilt, has explored how an early, negotiated end to the war might have resulted in an uncannily different 1970s England.

Although often associated with science fiction, alternative history is difficult to confine to a single genre. It has attracted literary novelists, as well as fantasy, young adult and steampunk authors. Its appeal lies not just in historical speculation, but in the opportunity to consider how conditions of life might change in this altered reality and what this may reveal about our understandings of human nature, society and history.

Counterfactual thinking

Alternative history fiction is often treated as a relatively contemporary form of speculation and storytelling. But the practice goes back to the entangled origins of literary and historical writing.

The roots of alternative history can be traced to Herodotus, whose Histories are regarded as foundational texts of the Western historical tradition. In addition to their detailed accounts of the rise of the Persian Empire and the Greco-Persian wars, they are notable for Herodotus’ explicit interest in providing explanations for the events he described.

Herodotus was arguably influenced by the storytelling traditions of his time and their preoccupation with divine fate and tragic inevitability. He describes a world where acts of kindness are met with gratitude, and wrongs are violently avenged. What results is a conception of history as a causal chain, where each event seeds the next.

This led Herodotus to contemplate the alternative possibilities that might follow from a single difference. At one point, he considers what might have occurred if the Athenians had refused to commit their fleet to the Greek alliance during the second Persian invasion of Greece, mounted by Xerxes I in 480 BCE.

Herodotus speculates that, if not for the naval strength of the Athenians and their crucial role in the Battle of Salamis in September 480, Xerxes would have been able to isolate and conquer the Greek city states by sea. By briefly describing the catastrophe that could have resulted from a different choice, Herodotus emphasises both the fragility of the Greek coalition and the decisive role he attributes to Athens in securing victory.
 
The Battle of Salamis – Wilhelm von Kaulbach (1868) Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

A similar strategy appeared centuries later in the work of Roman historian Livy. Livy briefly imagines a world in which Alexander the Great survives beyond his death in Babylon in 323 BCE and proceeds with his planned invasion of Europe. Livy argues that if he had done so, Alexander would probably have been defeated by Rome, then a relatively small and insignificant city state. This reinforced Livy’s assertions about Roman military superiority and political organisation.

In both cases, the alternative scenario is not an end in itself. Rather, it has an argumentative function. The speculation supports the author’s broader historical claims. The same logic underpins the opening of Regime Change. Haberman and Swan’s consideration of an alternative and more routine second term for Trump supports their contention that his time out of office motivated and enabled the radical upheavals that followed his return to the presidency.

Counterfactual histories

These kinds of speculative digressions are generally referred to as “counterfactual histories” when encountered in historical writing. They have appeared in histories for centuries, largely as occasional asides. But counterfactual histories became more prominent in the 20th century, with the emergence of popular essays and books that explicitly explored “what if” scenarios.

A key publication was If It Had Happened Otherwise, a 1931 collection of essays by prominent British and American historians, politicians and authors. The essays tended to be more whimsical than seriously analytic. Contributors explored implausible scenarios, like how a successful British General Strike in 1926 could have resulted in an oppressive communist regime, or how the poet Lord Byron, a military leader in Greek War of Independence, might have become the first king of an independent Greece if he had survived his 1824 illness.
 
Cover of If It Had Happened Otherwise, edited by J. C. Squire (Longmans, Green and Co., originally published in 1931).

The volume also included a famously odd double-counterfactual essay by Winston Churchill, If Lee Had Not Won the Battle at Gettysburg. Churchill wrote the essay from the perspective of a historian in an alternative Confederate States of America, wondering what might have occurred if the Union armies had won the American Civil War.

Perhaps the most influential defence of counterfactual history was provided by Cambridge sociologist Geoffrey Hawthorn in his 1993 book Plausible Worlds: Possibility and Understanding in History and the Social Sciences.

As well as exploring some intriguing scenarios (alternative histories of early modern Europe, 20th-century Korea, and painting in the Italian Renaissance), Hawthorn argues that asking what might have happened can improve our understanding of what did occur. Considering alternative outcomes highlights the importance of particular events and decisions, while challenging deterministic explanations of history. If history could have plausibly unfolded in different ways, then no single social theory can fully explain its course.

This argument proved particularly attractive to historians like Niall Ferguson. Following Hawthorn, Ferguson maintains that counterfactuals can be employed to critique overly deterministic (particularly Marxist) historical theories by demonstrating history could have unfolded very differently if a critical event had a different outcome. Further, counterfactuals emphasise the extent to which history is shaped by individual personalities and decisions, rather than monumental social forces.

Ferguson explores counterfactual scenarios in several of his popular histories, perhaps most controversially in The Pity of War: Explaining World War One. Here he describes an alternative history of Europe in which Britain remained neutral in 1914 and Germany emerged victorious, eventually ruling over a peacefully united continent.
 
Cover of Niall Ferguson’s The Pity of War (Penguin Books; originally published in 1998).

Ferguson uses this counterfactual history to deconstruct what he sees as some common “myths” about the war, particularly in relation to German militarism and aggression, and the necessity of Britain’s involvement. He argues the course of the conflict was not inevitable or preordained, as many historians seem to assume. With different decisions, it could have easily gone another way.

The role of counterfactual speculation in historical argument has also been critiqued. E.H. Carr famously dismissed counterfactuals as “parlour-games with might-have-beens”. But perhaps the most extensive critique is Richard J. Evans’ book Altered Pasts: Counterfactuals and History (2014).

Evans sees any attempt at rigour or logic in a counterfactual history as a pretence or veneer of respectability. Counterfactuals can be developed in ways that will support any historical claim or argument, reflecting the worst tendencies of postmodern historiography. As Evans puts it, “once you let the counterfactual genie out of the bag, anything can happen”.

Evans also contends that many counterfactual histories reveal more about the nostalgic desires or reactionary assumptions of their authors than about the past itself. Many scenarios in If It Had Happened Otherwise, for example, imagine a stronger or more enduring British Empire. Similar tendencies can be found across the political spectrum. Evans notes the fantasies of left-wing historians about what might have happened if Lenin had lived to lead the Soviet Union for longer.

Novelists attempt to depict the lived experience of a history that took another path. The strange and sometimes terrifying worlds they create invite us to reconsider the precarious and contingent nature of contemporary values, relationships, and forms of identity we may take for granted.

The enduring popularity of this kind of speculation in history and fiction suggests that imagining what might have been is an important way of making sense of the past and our relationship with it.

Regime Change, Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan’s account of the first year of Donald Trump’s historically unprecedented return to the United States presidency, begins with an intriguing detour. For several pages, the authors imagine an alternative history in which Trump won re-election in 2020 and commenced his second term in 2021 rather than 2025.

In this scenario, Trump emerges from his first administration more cautious and constrained, lacking the opportunity to galvanise supporters through claims of electoral theft and political persecution. As a result, the upheavals that characterised his eventual return to office never occur. Had the 2020 election produced a different result, Haberman and Swan speculate, we might now be living in a calmer and more predictable world.

This desire to consider alternative histories, how the world might have changed if a known event had a different outcome, is shared by novelists and historians. Yet they generally pursue different aims.

All approaches to alternative history begin with what writers and scholars often describe as a point of divergence: a plausible change to recorded events that could have created a different timeline.

The possibilities are almost endless. What if Adolf Hitler had been assassinated in 1943 rather than dying by suicide in 1945? What if the Soviet Union had reached the Moon before the US in 1969? What if smallpox had never devastated the Indigenous peoples of North America? What if Christopher Columbus had failed to reach the Americas in 1492, only for European societies to face an Incan invasion decades later?

From a single altered event, entirely different worlds may emerge.

Fictional alternatives

Alternative history fiction is built upon this premise. This subgenre can be identified in literature as early as 1490. The chivalric romance Tirant lo Blanc tells the story of a wandering knight who manages to prevent the fall of Constantinople and the destruction of the Byzantine Empire.

But alternative histories really take off in the 19th and 20th centuries. Authors were drawn to imagine the unfamiliar realities that might have resulted from, for example, Napoleon’s successful conquest of Europe, or a Confederate victory in the American Civil War.

The history of the second world war, in particular, frequently invites this kind of speculation. Philip K. Dick’s classic The Man in the High Castle describes a US partitioned between Nazi Germany and Imperial Japan after the Axis powers triumph.
 
Cover of Philip K. Dick’s The Man in the High Castle (Gollancz, SF Masterworks edition; originally published in 1962).

Robert Harris’ Fatherland similarly depicts a post-war Nazi regime, using the conventions of noir crime fiction to reveal the hidden atrocities of the German state, 20 years after its victory.

More recently, New Zealand author Catherine Chidgey, in her novel The Book of Guilt, has explored how an early, negotiated end to the war might have resulted in an uncannily different 1970s England.

Although often associated with science fiction, alternative history is difficult to confine to a single genre. It has attracted literary novelists, as well as fantasy, young adult and steampunk authors. Its appeal lies not just in historical speculation, but in the opportunity to consider how conditions of life might change in this altered reality and what this may reveal about our understandings of human nature, society and history.

Counterfactual thinking

Alternative history fiction is often treated as a relatively contemporary form of speculation and storytelling. But the practice goes back to the entangled origins of literary and historical writing.

The roots of alternative history can be traced to Herodotus, whose Histories are regarded as foundational texts of the Western historical tradition. In addition to their detailed accounts of the rise of the Persian Empire and the Greco-Persian wars, they are notable for Herodotus’ explicit interest in providing explanations for the events he described.

Herodotus was arguably influenced by the storytelling traditions of his time and their preoccupation with divine fate and tragic inevitability. He describes a world where acts of kindness are met with gratitude, and wrongs are violently avenged. What results is a conception of history as a causal chain, where each event seeds the next.

This led Herodotus to contemplate the alternative possibilities that might follow from a single difference. At one point, he considers what might have occurred if the Athenians had refused to commit their fleet to the Greek alliance during the second Persian invasion of Greece, mounted by Xerxes I in 480 BCE.

Herodotus speculates that, if not for the naval strength of the Athenians and their crucial role in the Battle of Salamis in September 480, Xerxes would have been able to isolate and conquer the Greek city states by sea. By briefly describing the catastrophe that could have resulted from a different choice, Herodotus emphasises both the fragility of the Greek coalition and the decisive role he attributes to Athens in securing victory.
 
The Battle of Salamis – Wilhelm von Kaulbach (1868) Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

A similar strategy appeared centuries later in the work of Roman historian Livy. Livy briefly imagines a world in which Alexander the Great survives beyond his death in Babylon in 323 BCE and proceeds with his planned invasion of Europe. Livy argues that if he had done so, Alexander would probably have been defeated by Rome, then a relatively small and insignificant city state. This reinforced Livy’s assertions about Roman military superiority and political organisation.

In both cases, the alternative scenario is not an end in itself. Rather, it has an argumentative function. The speculation supports the author’s broader historical claims. The same logic underpins the opening of Regime Change. Haberman and Swan’s consideration of an alternative and more routine second term for Trump supports their contention that his time out of office motivated and enabled the radical upheavals that followed his return to the presidency.

Counterfactual histories

These kinds of speculative digressions are generally referred to as “counterfactual histories” when encountered in historical writing. They have appeared in histories for centuries, largely as occasional asides. But counterfactual histories became more prominent in the 20th century, with the emergence of popular essays and books that explicitly explored “what if” scenarios.

A key publication was If It Had Happened Otherwise, a 1931 collection of essays by prominent British and American historians, politicians and authors. The essays tended to be more whimsical than seriously analytic. Contributors explored implausible scenarios, like how a successful British General Strike in 1926 could have resulted in an oppressive communist regime, or how the poet Lord Byron, a military leader in Greek War of Independence, might have become the first king of an independent Greece if he had survived his 1824 illness.
 
Cover of If It Had Happened Otherwise, edited by J. C. Squire (Longmans, Green and Co., originally published in 1931).

The volume also included a famously odd double-counterfactual essay by Winston Churchill, If Lee Had Not Won the Battle at Gettysburg. Churchill wrote the essay from the perspective of a historian in an alternative Confederate States of America, wondering what might have occurred if the Union armies had won the American Civil War.

Perhaps the most influential defence of counterfactual history was provided by Cambridge sociologist Geoffrey Hawthorn in his 1993 book Plausible Worlds: Possibility and Understanding in History and the Social Sciences.

As well as exploring some intriguing scenarios (alternative histories of early modern Europe, 20th-century Korea, and painting in the Italian Renaissance), Hawthorn argues that asking what might have happened can improve our understanding of what did occur. Considering alternative outcomes highlights the importance of particular events and decisions, while challenging deterministic explanations of history. If history could have plausibly unfolded in different ways, then no single social theory can fully explain its course.

Further, counterfactuals emphasise the extent to which history is shaped by individual personalities and decisions, rather than monumental social forces.

An open truck loaded with cattle passes by. They might have travelled a few hundred kilometres from a rural market to an urban centre, eventually ending up in a butcher’s shop to meet ever-growing urban demand. But the cattle have no idea; they seem to enjoy the free ride, as did the pigs in the film Babe: Pig in the City (1998). The cattle don't pay for the nice trip, and they get free food along the way. Will the cattle ever know they're actually products in this ruthless marketing chain, transported to the market for customers who pay for their travel, food and all other expenses?

Amused, you might quickly find an image or video clip of happy bovines on a moving truck on your favourite tech platform, such as Google, Facebook, YouTube or TikTok. You marvel at the technology, even though you pay nothing for these services. But have you ever thought that you might be the very cow these tech giants are transporting for free? Think about what other posts, articles, images, video clips or commercials appeared before you while you were browsing these search engines or social media marvels. If history is any guide, predatory commercial, territorial and colonial entities often come in disguise, and by the time their intentions become clear, it is too late. Research suggests that Britain drained nearly US$45 trillion from India between 1765 and 1938, while Indians remained largely unaware of the astronomical scale of this plunder. To put it in perspective, that is 17 times the United Kingdom's total annual gross domestic product today. We register for free services, unwittingly giving away personal data to big tech, only to become products in their colossal product line. They track our every step, every book we read, every film we watch, every website we visit, every trip we take, every doctor we see and even every message we send. We become encrypted entities in their massive databases, housed in cold data centres somewhere far away. Mere products. (Or are we inmates like ‘1084’ in Mahasweta Devi’s acclaimed book 1084’s Mother?)
An aerial view of an Amazon Web Services data centre (US East 1) in Ashburn, Virginia, on 20 October 2025. As tech giants pour billions into similar facilities across Southeast Asia, the promise of local job creation is increasingly overshadowed by serious concerns over water depletion and environmental degradation. Photo: Reuters

Google launched its search engine in September 1998 and acquired YouTube in October 2006. Facebook opened to the general public in September 2006. Netflix launched its online streaming service to the public on 16 January 2007. We all celebrated each event as a sign of human progress and embraced these developments with open arms. They all seemed like marvels that made work and life so much easier and more enjoyable. Little did we realise that we were gradually giving up our ability to think, argue, debate and reach well-considered conclusions on any issue. A small test will help us understand this.

Search Google, YouTube or Facebook for arguments supporting the claim, however ridiculous it may be, that the Earth is flat. Browse the results on each platform for a few minutes. You may soon notice that these platforms bring up more and more of these bizarre results, even when you search for an entirely different topic. Your homepage may become awash with claims that the Earth is flat, no matter how outlandish. Now imagine someone with a particular bias, be it racial, gender-based or otherwise, runs a search to find results reflecting that bias. They may be constantly fed articles, claims, video clips, images and whatnot that reinforce their bias, potentially turning it into a radical belief. This is artificial intelligence (AI) in action: reading your mind, knowing what you would like to see and curating a world of belief – an ‘echo chamber’ – just for you. ‘Truth’ becomes a personalised product; the same fact may appear differently to different people, depending on what they want to see, where they are and, above all, what the powerful political and tech elites behind the apps want them to think and believe.

The chain of events in Myanmar in the 2010s illustrates the point. Firebrand Buddhist monks repeatedly delivered speeches that dehumanised and denigrated minority Muslims. Their followers enthusiastically shared these speeches on Facebook. Its AI-driven algorithm, designed to promote content that attracts greater user engagement and thus generates more revenue, readily picked them up and spread them even further, regardless of whether those monks made true or false statements or promoted violence. We watched in utter disbelief as a new brand of Buddhism – ‘militant Buddhism’ – took shape within a religion whose core tenets include non-violence towards humans and animals. No harm should be done to others, not even to a tiny insect, and this is non-negotiable. However, the followers of these vitriolic monks quickly swelled in number, spreading more false stories and inciting further violence. This hatred spread like wildfire, contributing to gruesome war crimes and massacres of genocidal proportions and forcing more than 750,000 Rohingya to seek refuge across the border in Bangladesh.
Residents and rescuers search the rubble of the Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab, southern Iran, following a US missile strike on 28 February 2026 that killed 156 civilians. Investigations linked the tragedy to flawed intelligence, outdated imagery, and an overreliance on AI, raising urgent questions about legal accountability in autonomous warfare. Photo: Reuters

While we have already struggled to distinguish real from fake news because of the mass, indiscriminate proliferation of social media, AI-based large language models (LLMs) developed by companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and DeepSeek have made the situation even more alarming. We have outsourced our thinking, reading, analysis and writing to these models, leaving decision-making to soulless machines. Earlier this year, President Trump reportedly consulted Grok about the potential outcomes before launching his operation in Venezuela, in which American troops seized the country's president from his residence.

Then there are killer robots, formally known as lethal autonomous weapons systems (LAWS). Also known as slaughterbots, they use AI to identify, select and engage targets without human intervention. Conventional remotely operated military drones require a human operator to authorise an attack, whereas a slaughterbot can engage a target independently. But who takes legal responsibility if an innocent person is harmed by a slaughterbot? Its owner? Designer? Manufacturer? Software developer? Someone else? It gets dizzyingly complex.

This is precisely the kind of concern raised by the US military strike on Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab, southern Iran, on 28 February 2026, which killed civilians, including numerous schoolchildren. (Imagine little girls in school uniforms, carrying schoolbags, losing their lives in such horrific circumstances. I had to stop for a few minutes as my mind froze.) What subsequent investigations found was chilling. Flawed intelligence, outdated imagery and an alleged overreliance on AI contributed to this unimaginably gruesome tragedy. One report says US commanders ignored warnings before approving the strike that hit the girls’ school. A former Pentagon official claimed that faulty AI targeting was not to blame; rather, staff cuts and oversight failures were. The bottom line: no one has taken responsibility. Questions remain about whether existing legal mechanisms can effectively hold anyone accountable. Does this mean AI can kill and annihilate without anyone being held responsible? Is it above the law? But who owns AI technology and the LLMs? Who are the beneficiaries? Who is promoting it indiscriminately?
AI giant Anthropic agreed to pay $1.5 billion in compensation following a 2025 class-action copyright lawsuit by writers over the unauthorized use of millions of books and creative works to train its models, all while denying any wrongdoing. File Photo: Reuters

Here is another example that raises questions about the legal accountability of AI companies and their powerful technological and political backers. LLMs are aggressively gobbling up millions of books, paintings, musical compositions and other creative works for training (read: ‘copying’ and ‘mimicking’), often without permission. Fed up with what they regarded as a gross act of piracy, a group of writers pursued a class-action copyright lawsuit against AI giant Anthropic in the Northern District of California. In 2025, the company agreed to a US$1.5 billion settlement. But what is noteworthy is something else: Anthropic denied any wrongdoing! If there was no wrongdoing, why did Anthropic agree to pay such a substantial sum? What does this tell us about the legal boundaries of AI training and copyright protection? Are we supposed to accept that copyright infringement is not wrongdoing?

If the current legal framework allows AI giants, their owners and powerful users to evade accountability, what future can we expect? For one, no one may be held responsible for the Minab massacre, and similar incidents may recur. AI giants will continue to devour human creative work. Soulless machines will make decisions about human matters. Fatal errors and misjudgements will be met with the cold apathy of a seasoned politician or a tech oligarch.

Meanwhile, ordinary citizens will remain blissfully unaware that they are gradually handing everything over to these AI giants, happily consuming the leftovers of this voracious, all-engulfing technology. Simple AI tools for image creation, text generation or audio enhancement will keep them content. Students are using AI to write summaries of long, complex philosophical essays in an instant. Machines write public policy papers on fundamentally human issues, and no one gives them a second thought. LLMs write ‘creative’ literary works or ‘analytical’ articles, but in reality, they merely regurgitate what others have written before. Judges pretend to ‘deliberate’; doctors feign ‘diagnosing’ diseases, while LLMs housed in data centres far away in Indonesia or Brazil do the work. Fake and manipulative content, including images, audio and videos, is spreading everywhere; humans are hunched over their mobile phones or glued to TV screens, devouring whatever they display, unaware that their ability to think and their creative skills are rapidly eroding. This is end-times colonialism, borrowing from Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor’s recently published book End Times Fascism (published on 15 September 2026 by Farrar, Straus and Giroux).
Tobacco farmers in northern Bangladesh show hands stained dark with nicotine-rich sap, a visual reminder of "green tobacco sickness"—the hidden cost behind corporate-backed cash crops that mirrors the long-term toll of unchecked big tech. Photo: S Dilip Roy

But modern colonialism is clever. It entices you with happiness and immediate profits while keeping long-term harms hidden, much like tobacco farming promoted by large corporations in Bangladesh and many other developing countries. Tobacco cultivation typically requires fertile land and large quantities of chemical fertilisers. Big tobacco companies lure farmers with free seeds, chemical fertilisers, pesticides, interest-free loans and guaranteed buyback contracts. However, this farming practice severely reduces soil organic matter and the levels of nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and sulphur in tobacco-growing areas. Heavy chemical runoff also pollutes local canals and wetlands, harming native fish species. In addition, tobacco displaces alternative food and cash crops such as potatoes, pulses and mustard. Then there is green tobacco sickness, a form of nicotine poisoning that occurs when nicotine from wet tobacco leaves is absorbed through the skin. Children and women, particularly pregnant women and those who have recently given birth, are especially vulnerable. Yet the lure of immediate profits keeps farmers trapped in this devastating practice.

The rapid proliferation of data centres tells a similar story. They are spreading across Southeast Asia, backed by major investments from Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Oracle, Alibaba, ByteDance and others. They promise new jobs for local people, including technicians, builders, carpenters, plumbers and electricians, although actual job creation may fall considerably short of projections (only 25 percent of the jobs predicted in the UK, according to a Guardian report). However, whether or not new jobs materialise, data centres in the Indonesian city of Batam have reportedly contributed to severe water shortages, leaving residents struggling to meet basic needs such as cooking and showering. Such developments raise concerns about the region’s long-term ecological sustainability and habitability. ASEAN nations are scrambling to deal with this new economic force. How can they balance the lure of massive investment (US$160 billion from American tech giants alone) with the needs of local populations? They face a dilemma similar to that confronting tobacco farmers in northern Bangladesh. Preserve long-term health and well-being or prioritise immediate economic gains? Accept massive investments from tech giants or maintain the local environmental and ecological balance necessary to sustain life?
Cover of Brave New World by Aldous Huxley, first published in 1932.

History has repeatedly shown that a civilisation flourishes when it promotes free and critical thinking and declines when it fails to do so. Francis Fukuyama makes an interesting point in his book The Origins of Political Order (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2011). While Islamic civilisation was in its heyday from the 7th to the 15th centuries, Europe was gradually opening up to free thinking and debate and developing legal systems that fostered advances in science, technology, philosophy, art, literature and every other branch of human knowledge and creativity. Why did Islamic civilisation lose its pre-eminence while Europe eventually surpassed it? Fukuyama’s explanation includes the rule of law, the separation of church and state, the development of bureaucracy and the spread of education, all of which point to the ability to think critically, free from the fear of systematic state persecution and protected by law. Of course, this is an oversimplification, and Europe took centuries to reach that stage, but it captures the general path towards modernisation. European state formation was shaped not merely by military power but also by the development of institutions that enabled free and critical thinking.

If AI destroys humanity’s ability to think critically, we risk being dominated by a handful of tech and political masters, while most of us remain content as consumers of the leftovers. (British writer Aldous Huxley warned of a similar scenario in his dystopian science fiction novel Brave New World, published in London in 1932.) The worst part is that we won’t realise it. But what happens to those who promote unregulated AI, massive data centres and big tech’s godlike power? They might end up living on another planet, tailor-made to meet their every need. Watch Elysium (2013), directed by Neill Blomkamp, in which the very wealthy live on a man-made space station while the rest of the population lives on a ruined Earth.

Dr Sayeed Ahmed is the lead consultant at Sydney-based consultancy Tasman Analytics.

If history is any guide, predatory commercial, territorial and colonial entities often come in disguise, and by the time their intentions become clear, it is too late. Research suggests that Britain drained nearly US$45 trillion from India between 1765 and 1938, while Indians remained largely unaware of the astronomical scale of this plunder. To put it in perspective, that is 17 times the United Kingdom's total annual gross domestic product today. We register for free services, unwittingly giving away personal data to big tech, only to become products in their colossal product line. They track our every step, every book we read, every film we watch, every website we visit, every trip we take, every doctor we see and even every message we send. We become encrypted entities in their massive databases, housed in cold data centres somewhere far away. Mere products. (Or are we inmates like ‘1084’ in Mahasweta Devi’s acclaimed book 1084’s Mother?)
An aerial view of an Amazon Web Services data centre (US East 1) in Ashburn, Virginia, on 20 October 2025. As tech giants pour billions into similar facilities across Southeast Asia, the promise of local job creation is increasingly overshadowed by serious concerns over water depletion and environmental degradation. Photo: Reuters

Google launched its search engine in September 1998 and acquired YouTube in October 2006. Facebook opened to the general public in September 2006. Netflix launched its online streaming service to the public on 16 January 2007. We all celebrated each event as a sign of human progress and embraced these developments with open arms. They all seemed like marvels that made work and life so much easier and more enjoyable. Little did we realise that we were gradually giving up our ability to think, argue, debate and reach well-considered conclusions on any issue. A small test will help us understand this.

Search Google, YouTube or Facebook for arguments supporting the claim, however ridiculous it may be, that the Earth is flat. Browse the results on each platform for a few minutes. You may soon notice that these platforms bring up more and more of these bizarre results, even when you search for an entirely different topic. Your homepage may become awash with claims that the Earth is flat, no matter how outlandish. Now imagine someone with a particular bias, be it racial, gender-based or otherwise, runs a search to find results reflecting that bias. They may be constantly fed articles, claims, video clips, images and whatnot that reinforce their bias, potentially turning it into a radical belief. This is artificial intelligence (AI) in action: reading your mind, knowing what you would like to see and curating a world of belief – an ‘echo chamber’ – just for you. ‘Truth’ becomes a personalised product; the same fact may appear differently to different people, depending on what they want to see, where they are and, above all, what the powerful political and tech elites behind the apps want them to think and believe.

The chain of events in Myanmar in the 2010s illustrates the point. Firebrand Buddhist monks repeatedly delivered speeches that dehumanised and denigrated minority Muslims. Their followers enthusiastically shared these speeches on Facebook. Its AI-driven algorithm, designed to promote content that attracts greater user engagement and thus generates more revenue, readily picked them up and spread them even further, regardless of whether those monks made true or false statements or promoted violence. We watched in utter disbelief as a new brand of Buddhism – ‘militant Buddhism’ – took shape within a religion whose core tenets include non-violence towards humans and animals. No harm should be done to others, not even to a tiny insect, and this is non-negotiable. However, the followers of these vitriolic monks quickly swelled in number, spreading more false stories and inciting further violence. This hatred spread like wildfire, contributing to gruesome war crimes and massacres of genocidal proportions and forcing more than 750,000 Rohingya to seek refuge across the border in Bangladesh.
Residents and rescuers search the rubble of the Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab, southern Iran, following a US missile strike on 28 February 2026 that killed 156 civilians. Investigations linked the tragedy to flawed intelligence, outdated imagery, and an overreliance on AI, raising urgent questions about legal accountability in autonomous warfare. Photo: Reuters

While we have already struggled to distinguish real from fake news because of the mass, indiscriminate proliferation of social media, AI-based large language models (LLMs) developed by companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and DeepSeek have made the situation even more alarming. We have outsourced our thinking, reading, analysis and writing to these models, leaving decision-making to soulless machines. Earlier this year, President Trump reportedly consulted Grok about the potential outcomes before launching his operation in Venezuela, in which American troops seized the country's president from his residence.

Then there are killer robots, formally known as lethal autonomous weapons systems (LAWS). Also known as slaughterbots, they use AI to identify, select and engage targets without human intervention. Conventional remotely operated military drones require a human operator to authorise an attack, whereas a slaughterbot can engage a target independently. But who takes legal responsibility if an innocent person is harmed by a slaughterbot? Its owner? Designer? Manufacturer? Software developer? Someone else? It gets dizzyingly complex.

This is precisely the kind of concern raised by the US military strike on Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab, southern Iran, on 28 February 2026, which killed civilians, including numerous schoolchildren. (Imagine little girls in school uniforms, carrying schoolbags, losing their lives in such horrific circumstances. I had to stop for a few minutes as my mind froze.) What subsequent investigations found was chilling. Flawed intelligence, outdated imagery and an alleged overreliance on AI contributed to this unimaginably gruesome tragedy. One report says US commanders ignored warnings before approving the strike that hit the girls’ school. A former Pentagon official claimed that faulty AI targeting was not to blame; rather, staff cuts and oversight failures were. The bottom line: no one has taken responsibility. Questions remain about whether existing legal mechanisms can effectively hold anyone accountable. Does this mean AI can kill and annihilate without anyone being held responsible? Is it above the law? But who owns AI technology and the LLMs? Who are the beneficiaries? Who is promoting it indiscriminately?
AI giant Anthropic agreed to pay $1.5 billion in compensation following a 2025 class-action copyright lawsuit by writers over the unauthorized use of millions of books and creative works to train its models, all while denying any wrongdoing. File Photo: Reuters

Here is another example that raises questions about the legal accountability of AI companies and their powerful technological and political backers. LLMs are aggressively gobbling up millions of books, paintings, musical compositions and other creative works for training (read: ‘copying’ and ‘mimicking’), often without permission. Fed up with what they regarded as a gross act of piracy, a group of writers pursued a class-action copyright lawsuit against AI giant Anthropic in the Northern District of California. In 2025, the company agreed to a US$1.5 billion settlement. But what is noteworthy is something else: Anthropic denied any wrongdoing! If there was no wrongdoing, why did Anthropic agree to pay such a substantial sum? What does this tell us about the legal boundaries of AI training and copyright protection? Are we supposed to accept that copyright infringement is not wrongdoing?

If the current legal framework allows AI giants, their owners and powerful users to evade accountability, what future can we expect? For one, no one may be held responsible for the Minab massacre, and similar incidents may recur. AI giants will continue to devour human creative work. Soulless machines will make decisions about human matters. Fatal errors and misjudgements will be met with the cold apathy of a seasoned politician or a tech oligarch.

Meanwhile, ordinary citizens will remain blissfully unaware that they are gradually handing everything over to these AI giants, happily consuming the leftovers of this voracious, all-engulfing technology. Simple AI tools for image creation, text generation or audio enhancement will keep them content. Students are using AI to write summaries of long, complex philosophical essays in an instant. Machines write public policy papers on fundamentally human issues, and no one gives them a second thought. LLMs write ‘creative’ literary works or ‘analytical’ articles, but in reality, they merely regurgitate what others have written before. Judges pretend to ‘deliberate’; doctors feign ‘diagnosing’ diseases, while LLMs housed in data centres far away in Indonesia or Brazil do the work. Fake and manipulative content, including images, audio and videos, is spreading everywhere; humans are hunched over their mobile phones or glued to TV screens, devouring whatever they display, unaware that their ability to think and their creative skills are rapidly eroding. This is end-times colonialism, borrowing from Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor’s recently published book End Times Fascism (published on 15 September 2026 by Farrar, Straus and Giroux).

But modern colonialism is clever. It entices you with happiness and immediate profits while keeping long-term harms hidden, much like tobacco farming promoted by large corporations in Bangladesh and many other developing countries. Tobacco cultivation typically requires fertile land and large quantities of chemical fertilisers. The rapid proliferation of data centres tells a similar story. They are spreading across Southeast Asia, backed by major investments from Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Oracle, Alibaba, ByteDance and others. They promise new jobs for local people, including technicians, builders, carpenters, plumbers and electricians, although actual job creation may fall considerably short of projections (only 25 percent of the jobs predicted in the UK, according to a Guardian report). Accept massive investments from tech giants or maintain the local environmental and ecological balance necessary to sustain life?

History has repeatedly shown that a civilisation flourishes when it promotes free and critical thinking and declines when it fails to do so. Francis Fukuyama makes an interesting point in his book The Origins of Political Order (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2011). While Islamic civilisation was in its heyday from the 7th to the 15th centuries, Europe was gradually opening up to free thinking and debate and developing legal systems that fostered advances in science, technology, philosophy, art, literature and every other branch of human knowledge and creativity. Why did Islamic civilisation lose its pre-eminence while Europe eventually surpassed it? Fukuyama’s explanation includes the rule of law, the separation of church and state, the development of bureaucracy and the spread of education, all of which point to the ability to think critically, free from the fear of systematic state persecution and protected by law. European state formation was shaped not merely by military power but also by the development of institutions that enabled free and critical thinking.

If AI destroys humanity’s ability to think critically, we risk being dominated by a handful of tech and political masters, while most of us remain content as consumers of the leftovers. (British writer Aldous Huxley warned of a similar scenario in his dystopian science fiction novel Brave New World, published in London in 1932.) The worst part is that we won’t realise it. Watch Elysium (2013), directed by Neill Blomkamp, in which the very wealthy live on a man-made space station while the rest of the population lives on a ruined Earth.

Dr Sayeed Ahmed is the lead consultant at Sydney-based consultancy Tasman Analytics.

item.title: The Daily Star – Beyond microcredit: What Bangladesh’s poor really need
item.description:
Jonathan Morduch, professor of public policy and economics at New York University's Wagner Graduate School of Public Service and co-author of Portfolios of the Poor, has studied how low-income households in Bangladesh manage their finances since the early 1990s. In an interview with The Daily Star, he reflects on nearly five decades of microfinance in Bangladesh, its achievements and limitations, the transformative role of migration, remittances and the garment industry in reducing poverty, and why the next chapter of financial inclusion must focus on savings, flexibility and consumer protection.

The Daily Star (TDS): Bangladesh has nearly five decades of experience with microfinance. Looking back, what has microfinance actually achieved, and how does that differ from what it originally promised?

Jonathan Morduch (JM): It is actually a complicated question. Microcredit began with a very strong promise and a very strong narrative, built around a story that Muhammad Yunus told many times about working with a small group in a village outside his university in Chittagong. It highlighted the possibility that even poor people could borrow money, repay it and have entrepreneurial ambitions.
Professor Jonathan Morduch

That narrative was very successful in selling Grameen, both within Bangladesh and outside it. Donors were looking for ways to help reduce poverty, but they worried that if they just gave money to poor people, it would be wasted, used inefficiently or corruptly, or worse. Yunus's narrative pushed back against that. It was very clever because the fact that the money was going to women and that they were paying it back suggested they were doing something meaningful with it. Some people call it “the market test”. It has been criticised, but it was a very powerful piece of logic.

I think it was also problematic. To judge the success or failure of microcredit, you have to look not at how it was sold internationally and domestically, but at what it really did. When researchers asked borrowers what they were really doing with the money they borrowed, they often replied that they had used the loan to pay school fees, to buy grain for the coming season, to save a little or to pay off a different loan. Maybe half the time or more, these were not business activities.

So, in a real sense, the great contribution of microcredit was to provide liquidity: to bring money to people who were struggling just to manage their finances and meet their basic needs in a very unstable environment. That is a more complicated message to sell, internationally or even domestically, but it is truer to how people use microfinance. In that sense, we wouldn't expect microfinance to revolutionise or transform people's lives, but it could still make a difference.

One more thing is often missed in evaluations of whether microfinance worked or not: microcredit was a remarkable achievement in creating a reliable institution in villages that were not well served. The staff would show up at the right time with the right amount of money. They would promise a loan, deliver that loan, and people could count on it. At a time when electricity and many other services were not particularly reliable, that level of reliability was no small thing. And once that structure was built, BRAC and others could start layering other services onto it.

So, looking back, microcredit had many successes that would have been hard to imagine beforehand. I just don't think they were the successes that were popularised internationally.

TDS: Why has microfinance not delivered the entrepreneurial transformation it originally promised, despite reaching millions of people?

JM: Because I think most people were not looking for that kind of transformation. Yunus, I think, still strongly believes that everyone can be an entrepreneur. He himself is a brilliant entrepreneur and institution builder. But a lot of people don't want to start their own businesses. It's difficult, and they don't share the kind of ambition that he himself exhibits.

One reason microcredit was transformative is that customers were looking for a different kind of service, and they found it in microcredit. The promise was misaligned with what customers actually wanted. But that doesn't make it a failure. It makes it a different kind of proposition.
A woman trained by a local NGO makes dolls using jute and other plant fibres to earn a living. Microcredit can help small-scale producers invest when economic opportunities arise. Photo: Prabir Das

People can use microcredit for lots of things, and part of the answer lies in the structure of microcredit lending. Whether it is Grameen, BRAC or ASA, the structure is very similar: you borrow an amount of money and repay it in small instalments. In many ways, it was a stroke of genius to do it that way, because people can repay very easily in small sums rather than in one large sum at the end.

On the other hand, it is a very strange way to make a business loan. Usually, a business owner would borrow money, go away for a few months, develop their business, earn some profit and repay the loan at the end of, say, six months. If instead I said, “Look, I'm going to give you this loan, and I need you to start repaying it next week”, you might accept it if that were the only kind of loan you could get. But it is a really strange system for what is described as a business loan.

What the structure did, though (and I don't think this story is well told), was allow people to borrow for many purposes. That instalment pattern looks like a consumer loan, not a producer loan. When I make a purchase on my credit card, I repay it month by month; that is how a lot of consumer finance works. That structure allowed people to feel comfortable borrowing to buy food, to buy medicine and to do many things that simply helped them manage their lives better, knowing they could repay in instalments.
Workers sew clothes on the production floor of a garment factory in Bangladesh. The garment industry and remittances have played a transformative role in improving the livelihoods of low-income households. Photo: Sourav Hossain Siam

The second thing the structure did was allow people to repay not from the profits of a business but from the income coming into the household. The son has some work, the daughter has some work, the husband has some work. There are regular flows of income, and those flows can go towards repaying the loan.

So, are these outcomes systemic? It was not inevitable that people would use microfinance for all kinds of purposes, but when you look closely at what actually happens, the design enables it. In fact, it is well designed for it. That story is often hidden. But it works for the microlenders because it gives them a much bigger customer base. And it is often exactly what customers want and need.

TDS: Your research suggests that conventional poverty measures can overlook periods of deprivation within a year. How should this understanding inform the design of microfinance products and the assessment of their impact?

JM: The year-long microcredit loan with instalments is well designed for lots of purposes, but not for situations characterised by crises and recurrent risks. It is quite structured. That is an advantage most of the time, but in a crisis, it offers very little flexibility. People then need to borrow from another source to repay the loan. That can be a real problem with microcredit.

So one answer is to design financial products with more flexibility built in. There is research showing that when people have access to a product that lets them skip a few instalments and pay later, they actually do better. They invest more, and the product better fits their needs.

More broadly, that part of my work was inspired by the fact that many studies look at outcomes before and after and say, “Look, microcredit was not transformative; it didn't change poverty.” But that is partly because poverty is usually measured by average annual consumption. Microcredit may actually have been helping people reduce their exposure to poverty during the year, even if their average consumption did not rise. This is because it lets people save more easily or borrow ahead of a coming lean season. In that way, it can address poverty by helping people protect themselves in difficult times. I think that could be encouraged rather than hidden behind the narrative of transformation.

TDS: How have migration, remittances and the garment industry transformed rural Bangladesh, and what role has microfinance played in that transformation?

JM: I think the real transformation may come from a different direction. Microcredit and similar interventions started with the logic that rural poverty should be addressed by putting more resources directly into rural areas. But many rural workers themselves said: actually, I want to leave home and find a job in the city, where there are steadier and better-paying jobs. So, from the household's perspective, the question is not just how to increase earnings in villages. It is how a household can increase its resources through a range of strategies, which can involve migration, with remittances then sent back home.

For a long time, a big story in villages has been remittances, not just from abroad but also from within Bangladesh. That can be much more transformative than anything else going on. But something else has happened too. As the ready-made garment (RMG) sector grew, the government had more resources and became more ambitious, and you started to see roads and other infrastructure being built. That in itself creates and strengthens markets, which in turn creates jobs. The construction of roads, new government buildings and other offices also creates jobs for both men and women.
Migrant workers wait at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka following flight cancellations and delays. Despite their transformative contribution to Bangladesh’s economy through remittances, migrant workers often face considerable hardship and remain insufficiently recognised. Photo: Anisur Rahman

The remittance revolution in Bangladesh and the RMG sector have both been fairly pro-poor, surprisingly. That could not be taken for granted, and I think it is what has really transformed areas that were extremely poor before. It is not just the direct impacts but also the spillover effects: they generate more economic activity, more tax revenue and other kinds of investment, and the effects build over time. Microcredit, in that context, helps people manage these changes and take advantage of them: to migrate more easily or to invest a bit more when an opportunity arises. But it is not driving these processes. It is helping people tap into them.

TDS: What should Bangladesh prioritise to make economic growth more inclusive and reduce poverty?

JM: If you look at the data across countries, the biggest driver of poverty reduction has been economic growth. We see this in China, in India and in Bangladesh. But even if the data show the importance of growth very clearly, it is not so simple. You don't just flip a switch and growth happens. So-called “inclusive growth” is even harder.

One way to think about the economic transformations in Bangladesh is to imagine an engine that is creating jobs and opportunities, together with institutions like microfinance that help people take steps on their own: to migrate, to send remittances back home and to take up jobs in cities. Then, as jobs and growth build, those institutions help people tap into that process more effectively and cope with the risks it creates. That requires financial tools, not to build a business, but perhaps to build up enough savings for a family member to move to Dhaka and take advantage of the new economy.

That cannot be taken for granted. You need growth, but you also need a way for a broad group of people to take advantage of it. Otherwise, growth happens and only richer people benefit, or growth itself may not gain momentum. In many ways, it is low-income Bangladeshis who have driven this period of growth. They provided the labour that generated the remittances and helped build the RMG sector. I think the country really owes a debt to people who have been working very, very hard for their own sake, often in difficult conditions, and in the process have been building the country.
One of microcredit’s most significant achievements in Bangladesh has been the establishment of reliable financial institutions in rural communities that were previously underserved. Illustration: Salman Sakib Shahryar

TDS: What financial services and protections should Bangladesh prioritise to better serve low-income households?

JM: I have two priorities. The first is savings. We are already seeing the use of microcredit decline, especially after the pandemic, because people are asking: Why am I paying all this money to borrow when I could be saving on my own? So helping people save is a natural step beyond credit. In the beginning, when Yunus and others started, saving just wasn't seen as interesting or possible. But as we have come to understand what people's lives are really like, we have seen that people do want to save, and they can save. They need to save and borrow at the same time, and the mix now seems to be shifting more towards saving.

The second is consumer protection of all kinds, but especially in digital finance. I have just been in villages in the north, and everyone has a story of a scam that directly affected them or a close relative. It is keeping people from using these services, and it creates a lot of uncertainty. It may be their last Tk 2,000 or Tk 10,000, sometimes more. If you are well off, that may not be much money. But if you are struggling in a village, it can be a lot of money to lose, with no means of getting it back.

So protections and regulations that ensure accountability on the part of providers, make it easier to seek redress and help people know where to turn when problems arise are all very important steps.

The interview was conducted by Khairul Hassan Jahin and Musrat Hossain Mithila.

It is how a household can increase its resources through a range of strategies, which can involve migration, with remittances then sent back home.

But something else has happened too. As the ready-made garment (RMG) sector grew, the government had more resources and became more ambitious, and you started to see roads and other infrastructure being built. Microcredit, in that context, helps people manage these changes and take advantage of them: to migrate more easily or to invest a bit more when an opportunity arises. But it is not driving these processes. It is helping people tap into them.

JM: If you look at the data across countries, the biggest driver of poverty reduction has been economic growth. We see this in China, in India and in Bangladesh. That requires financial tools, not to build a business, but perhaps to build up enough savings for a family member to move to Dhaka and take advantage of the new economy.

That cannot be taken for granted. You need growth, but you also need a way for a broad group of people to take advantage of it. Otherwise, growth happens and only richer people benefit, or growth itself may not gain momentum. In many ways, it is low-income Bangladeshis who have driven this period of growth. They provided the labour that generated the remittances and helped build the RMG sector. I think the country really owes a debt to people who have been working very, very hard for their own sake, often in difficult conditions, and in the process have been building the country.
One of microcredit’s most significant achievements in Bangladesh has been the establishment of reliable financial institutions in rural communities that were previously underserved. Illustration: Salman Sakib Shahryar
