item.title: The Daily Star – Afterlife of political power: Children of Bangladesh’s fallen establishment
item.description:
Political upheaval does not end when a government falls. For the children of those who once occupied positions of influence, its consequences can follow them across borders, into universities, relationships and the consulting room.

As a psychiatrist working in Australia, including with people from migrant and diaspora communities, I have increasingly encountered young Bangladeshis whose personal circumstances have been shaped by the political upheaval of recent years. Some are international students. Their immediate concerns may appear familiar: relationships, anxiety, substance use, identity and the challenges of establishing themselves in a new country. Yet behind these ordinary difficulties can lie an unusually complicated family history.

When Sheikh Hasina’s government collapsed in August 2024, it marked the end of more than a decade of political dominance. Hasina fled to India in the wake of student-led protests and the violent confrontations that followed. The consequences have extended well beyond Bangladesh. Families associated with the former administration have dispersed across the world. Some have sought refuge in neighbouring countries, while others have established themselves in Britain, Australia, Canada and elsewhere. For some, this movement represents political survival; for others, it may involve the preservation of wealth, educational opportunities and family security following a dramatic loss of influence.

The following portraits, using pseudonyms and deliberately altered or blended details, illustrate some of the themes I have encountered. They are not intended as identifiable clinical case histories.

Consider Janak, a young international student whose family was once associated with a prominent political establishment in Bangladesh. His parents have now left the country and are living elsewhere in the region. He is preoccupied with questions of status and family reputation. There is a sense that the family has experienced a humiliating reversal of fortune: people who once occupied positions of influence are now dispersed, anxious about their future and separated from the country in which their standing was established.
Children may find themselves managing the emotional consequences of their parents’ political experiences, even when they have little control over the events themselves. Photo: Collected/Unsplash

Janak has another problem. He has developed a significant dependence on cannabis but finds it almost impossible to acknowledge that he has an addiction. The word itself seems to represent an intolerable loss of status. In his understanding, addiction is associated with personal failure, weakness and social disgrace. His reluctance to accept the terminology makes it difficult to engage him in treatment.

This is not simply a case of an individual resisting a psychiatric label. In many South Asian communities, mental illness and substance dependence carry considerable stigma. Family reputation, educational achievement and the appearance of personal success are particularly important. Acknowledging a drug problem may feel like admitting a failure that extends beyond the individual to the family.

Janak’s predicament suggests a collision between two threatened identities: the loss of inherited family status and the fear of acquiring a new, stigmatised personal identity. The young man who cannot bear to be regarded as an addict may also be struggling to understand what remains of the identity his family once provided.

A second young person, whom I will call Shapna, presents a different dilemma. She is studying at a Sydney university and has established a social circle, largely among other Bangladeshis. She has a social media presence that connects her to people back home and has spent time living in different countries. Her father, a senior figure associated with the former political establishment, appears to have considerable wealth, the origins of which she does not fully understand.

Shapna seems conscious that her family’s financial circumstances are not straightforward. She has suspicions about the origins of some of her father’s money, but she also benefits from the family’s resources. She feels sympathy for her parents, who have been displaced from Bangladesh, and wants to support them. There is no simple way for her to separate affection for her family from questions about the legitimacy of its wealth.

This is an uncomfortable moral position, although not an unusual one in families where wealth and political influence have been intertwined. Children are rarely responsible for the circumstances in which their parents accumulated their fortunes. Nor should they automatically be expected to reject the material benefits of family life. But they may find themselves living with an uneasy awareness that the advantages they enjoy could have been acquired through improper means.
Protesters gather at Ganabhaban, the prime minister’s official residence in Dhaka, following the fall of Sheikh Hasina’s government on 5 August 2024. The consequences of this loss of political power extend well beyond Bangladesh. Photo: AFP

There is a useful international parallel here. In a 2021 report for the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, researcher Matthew Page examined the overseas education of children of politically exposed persons from West Africa, particularly Nigeria and Ghana. He identified at least 100 children of politically exposed persons who were attending or had recently attended British educational institutions. The report raised concerns that some tuition payments might involve unexplained or illicit wealth. It also explored how elite families use international education to reproduce social status, establish networks and protect their children’s futures.

This is relevant to Bangladesh. Our universities and financial institutions are not the only places where the consequences of political patronage can be felt. The international education system, property markets and financial networks can all become destinations for wealth accumulated in circumstances that deserve scrutiny. This is not an accusation against individual students but a broader question about the relationship between international mobility, family privilege and the preservation of wealth.

A third experience involves a Bangladeshi-Australian woman, whom I will call Mira. She married a man she had met during her university studies without initially appreciating the extent of his family’s political connections. Only later did she discover that he was closely associated with a prominent political family. Following the political upheaval in Bangladesh, her husband has gone into hiding in Dhaka, fearing for his safety. She remains in Sydney with their young child.

She has expressed sympathy for the former government, arguing that the extent of its corruption has been exaggerated and expressing enthusiasm about the possibility of Sheikh Hasina returning to Bangladesh. She also draws comparisons with Australian politics, pointing to scandals and questionable conduct among Australian politicians. There is perhaps an understandable instinct to temper accusations against one’s own family by pointing to the imperfections of other political systems.

These experiences invite a broader consideration of what might be called the psychological afterlife of political power. The fall of a government may be a discrete historical event, but for families associated with it, the consequences can persist for years. The loss of status, uncertainty surrounding wealth, fear of political retribution and the need to reconstruct identity do not disappear when someone crosses an international border.

The sociologist Arlie Hochschild’s concept of emotion work offers one way of understanding this process. In a 2025 study in the Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies, Verónica Díaz Cerda examined the experiences of children of Chilean political exiles, including those born in Britain to parents who had fled the Pinochet dictatorship. She described how children sometimes suppressed or evoked particular emotions to maintain a semblance of normality within families whose lives had been fractured by exile. They became agents of care, attempting to repair the emotional world of their parents, sometimes at the cost of their own emotional well-being. Although the circumstances of Chilean political refugees differ substantially from those of the children of Bangladesh’s former ruling establishment, the idea of emotion work is illuminating. Children can become responsible for managing the emotional consequences of their parents’ political experiences, even when they have little control over the events themselves.
For children of former political elites, the ordinary demands of young adulthood may be compounded by a parent’s loss of power, uncertainty surrounding family wealth or a political history that is difficult to discuss.

There is a further historical dimension in Bangladesh. The country’s 1971 Liberation War remains a powerful part of the identity of many families. For some parents who participated in or were deeply affected by the liberation struggle, the events of that period have never entirely receded into history. Their children may inherit not simply stories of national independence but also the emotional and political loyalties associated with it. In some families, political identity is transmitted almost as a form of inheritance. The events of 2024, however, have created a new rupture, involving a younger generation whose experience of Bangladesh may increasingly be shaped by displacement and distance.

Even the Bangladeshi diaspora in the West has felt the repercussions. Tulip Siddiq, the British Labour MP and niece of Sheikh Hasina, resigned as a Treasury minister in January 2025 after questions arose about London properties associated with members of her family and people connected to the former Bangladeshi government. She maintained that she had done nothing wrong. The episode nevertheless illustrated how the political history of Bangladesh could reach into the professional and public lives of people who had built careers abroad.

The future remains uncertain. Hasina has continued to indicate that she intends to return to Bangladesh. In an interview with the Associated Press in November 2026, she reiterated her intention to return in December, despite having been sentenced to death in absentia in 2025 over the crackdown on protesters. She disputes the verdict and the legitimacy of the proceedings. Whether she returns or not, the possibility itself has significance for families divided between Bangladesh and their new countries of residence. It keeps alive the sense that the political story is not finished and that the fortunes of those associated with the former government may change again.

These circumstances offer a reminder that mental health cannot always be understood solely in terms of an individual’s immediate circumstances. Anxiety, addiction, depression and difficulties with identity may be connected to a family history that is politically complicated, morally ambiguous and sometimes deliberately concealed. The patient sitting in front of us may be negotiating not only the ordinary demands of young adulthood but also the emotional consequences of a parent’s loss of power, a family’s uncertain wealth or a political history that is difficult to discuss.

Perhaps the most interesting feature of this generation is the tension between inherited privilege and inherited uncertainty. The children of political elites may retain their education, wealth and international connections but lose the certainty that once accompanied their family name. They must negotiate a new identity in countries that offer freedom and opportunity while carrying the unresolved history of a political establishment whose fate remains contested.

Political power is usually studied through the actions of leaders, institutions and movements. Its aftermath deserves to be examined through the experiences of families who inherit its consequences. The fall of Sheikh Hasina’s government was a defining moment in Bangladesh’s modern history. For some younger members of the Bangladeshi diaspora, however, the event is not simply something that happened in their country of origin. It is something they continue to live with, in their relationships, their identities and sometimes in the consulting room.

Dr Tanveer Ahmed is a Sydney-based psychiatrist and author. He can be reached at [email protected].

item.title: The Daily Star – Sher-e-Bangla A K Fazlul Huq: Revisiting a complex legacy
item.description: One of the most influential political figures in the history of Bengal, Sher-e-Bangla A K Fazlul Huq left an enduring legacy through his advocacy for peasant rights, his challenge to entrenched political and economic power, and his role in shaping the politics of colonial and postcolonial Bengal. Yet his political thought, achievements and contradictions deserve renewed attention beyond familiar historical narratives. Through a collection of essays and historical analyses, The Daily Star's Slow Reads revisits his life, political struggles, ideas and legacy, exploring how his vision and actions shaped Bengal's past and continue to resonate in Bangladesh today.

item.title: The Daily Star – How Sufism and shrine veneration shaped Muslim society in the Bengal delta
item.description:
The process of Islamisation in the Bengal delta was complex, shaped by the region’s pre-existing religious and cultural beliefs and practices. Early Sufis and mystics played a significant role in spreading Islam throughout the region. By establishing khanqahs (Sufi lodges), dargahs (shrines), and mosques, early Sufis helped mediate the relationship between Islamic teachings and the diverse religious and cultural environment. Shrine-centred devotional practices, the veneration of pirs (spiritual masters), and the circulation of vernacular religious literature contributed to the emergence of distinctive forms of Bengali Muslim religious expression.

It has been argued that, even before the establishment of Mughal hegemony, there was scarcely a locality in Bengal without a shrine. A fifteenth-century letter attributed to Mir Sayyid Ashraf Jahangir Simnani (d. 1425), addressed to Sultan Ibrahim Sharqi of Jaunpur (d. 1440?), captures the extent of Sufi influence in Bengal: "In short, in the country of Bengal, what to speak of the cities, there is no town and no village where holy saints did not come and settle down" (quoted in Karim, Social History of the Muslims in Bengal (Down to A. D. 1538), 1985, p. 116). Although this statement should be understood as a representation of the widespread reputation of Sufi saints rather than a literal demographic record, it illustrates the significance attributed to their presence in the region.

The widespread veneration of Sufi saints has frequently led scholars to associate the Islamisation of the Bengal delta with Sufi missionary activity. Yet the historical formation of Muslim society cannot be explained through conversion narratives alone. It involved political transformations, agrarian expansion, settlement patterns, institutional developments, religious encounters, and the production of new forms of religious knowledge. This paper examines these interconnected processes through the historical development of Sufism and shrine-centred religious practices in Bengal. Drawing particularly on the works of Asim Roy, Richard M. Eaton, and Ayesha A. Irani, it argues that Bengali Islam emerged through the interaction of social and geographical transformations, localised religious practices, and vernacular intellectual production.

The geographical territories that constitute the Bengal delta were historically divided into several overlapping regions, including Raṛḥa, Gauṛa, Vanga, Samatata, Harikela, Pundra, and Varendra (Ramesh C. Majumdar, 1971, History of Ancient Bengal; Niharranjan Ray, 1949, Bangalir Itihas: Adi Parbo). Archaeological evidence suggests that Bengal was inhabited from prehistoric times, while its population and cultural formations developed through successive migrations, political expansions, and interactions among indigenous and external communities. 
Devotees carry ceremonial cloths (gilafs) during the annual Urs of Hazrat Shah Jalal in Sylhet, reflecting the enduring significance of Sufi shrine veneration in Bangladesh’s religious and cultural life. Photo: Star

The region experienced several phases of political consolidation before the arrival of Muslim rulers. Chandragupta, the Pala ruler Gopala, and the Sena ruler Vijayasena each contributed to the political integration of parts of Bengal at different historical moments. The conquest of Bengal by Ikhtiyaruddin Muhammad bin Bakhtiyar Khalji in 1204 marked the beginning of sustained Muslim political dominance in the region. It also facilitated the movement of Muslim scholars, administrators, merchants, preachers, and wandering dervishes into Bengal. Nevertheless, the expansion of Islam was neither immediate nor uniform. The emergence of Muslim communities was a prolonged process involving political authority, institutional patronage, settlement, agrarian development, and religious interaction.

Muslim contact with Bengal, however, predated the establishment of Muslim political dominance. Arab merchants visited the coastal regions of the Bay of Bengal from the early medieval period, and commercial networks may have facilitated the circulation of Islamic ideas and practices. Some scholars have also suggested that Muslim religious figures visited or settled in Bengal before the thirteenth-century conquest, although the chronology and historical evidence associated with several early Sufi figures remain uncertain.

Among the figures traditionally associated with the early history of Sufism in Bengal are Shah Sultan Rumi, Shaikh Ahmad or Abbas ibn Hamza Nishapuri, Shah Sultan Balkhi, Baba Adam Shahid, Shah Makhdum, and Shaykh Jalal al-Din Tabrizi. Regional traditions associate Shah Sultan Rumi with Netrakona, Shah Sultan Balkhi with Bogra, Shah Makhdum with Rajshahi, and Baba Adam Shahid with Vikrampura. Shaykh Jalal al-Din Tabrizi, associated with the Suhrawardiyya order, is traditionally connected with the early establishment of Sufi networks in Bengal. These accounts demonstrate the importance of saintly genealogies and local memory in the construction of Bengal's sacred geography, although individual dates and details of these figures' lives require careful historical verification.

The relationship between local religio-cultural traditions and the process of Islamisation in Bengal has been interpreted through several complementary historical, literary, and anthropological approaches. Asim Roy's The Islamic Syncretistic Tradition in Bengal (1983) focuses on the cultural and religious processes through which Islam developed a distinctive Bengali expression.

Roy argues that Bengali Islam emerged through sustained interaction between Islamic religious traditions and the existing cultural and religious practices of Bengal. This relationship became increasingly contested in subsequent periods.

Its appeal among the Muslim peasantry was connected with the social and economic conditions of rural Bengal, particularly the unequal distribution of land and the burdens associated with existing systems of rent and taxation.

The Tariqa-i Muhammadiyya and Tayyuni movements also contributed to debates about Islamic orthodoxy and religious practice. Although they differed in their doctrinal positions, political orientations, and attitudes towards congregational worship, they shared criticisms of certain popular devotional practices. Their disagreements also concerned the legal and political status of British-ruled India and the obligations of Muslims living under non-Muslim political authority (Muinuddin Ahmed Khan, History of the Fara’idi Movement in Bengal (1818–1906), 1965, pp. 89–103).

These movements sought to privilege scriptural interpretation, obligatory religious observance, and reformist scholarship over certain established forms of popular devotional authority. Their criticism did not necessarily eliminate Sufi institutions, but it changed the terms through which shrine veneration and saintly authority were publicly contested.

In the twentieth century, Tablighi Jama'at and other reform-oriented movements contributed to the continuing debate over the legitimacy of popular Sufi practices. In contemporary Bangladesh, these debates are also reflected in the positions of various Islamist and Salafi-oriented groups, including Jamaat-e-Islami and other religious organisations.

In conclusion, we may say that the history of Sufism in the Bengal delta demonstrates that the Islamisation of the region was neither a singular historical event nor a straightforward process of religious conversion. It involved the transformation of landscapes, the expansion of agricultural settlements, the establishment of religious institutions, the development of devotional practices, and the production of vernacular Islamic knowledge. The persistence of shrine-centred religious life alongside reformist challenges demonstrates that the history of Bengali Islam is not merely a history of conversion but also a history of the continuous negotiation of religious identity, authority, and belonging.

One of the most significant features of Saiyad Sultan's work is his use of the Vaiṣṇava concept of aṃśāvatāra, or partial divine manifestation, to explain Muhammad's primordial relationship with Allah. Through this conceptual framework, Muhammad is presented in terms intelligible to Bengali readers familiar with Indic theological ideas, while his distinctive status within Islamic prophetic history is maintained (2021, pp. 39–40).

Through the Nabīvaṃśa, Saiyad Sultan attempted to localise Islam by presenting Muhammad in the form of Viṣṇu's kalki avatar in a landscape deeply rooted in the traditions of Gauṛiya Vaiṣṇavism. Thus, Sultan portrayed Islam not as a new religion but rather as the local population's longstanding religious tradition. By integrating Hindu deities and sacred texts into Islamic prophetology, Saiyad Sultan implicitly expands the Qur’anic concept of the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab) to encompass the Hindu communities of Bengal.

Irani's contribution is particularly important for reconsidering Roy's concept of syncretism. Whereas Roy emphasises the absorption and reinterpretation of local cultural materials within Bengali Islam, Irani directs attention to the literary and theological strategies through which Islamic knowledge was translated into Bengali. The vernacular text did not merely reflect an already established Muslim identity; it actively participated in constructing the intellectual and religious categories through which Bengali Muslims could understand Islamic sacred history. An example of such an attempt is Sultan's use of the term Prabhu Niranjan, rather than Allah, to refer to the Creator.

The difference between the two approaches should not be overstated. Both recognise the importance of Bengali literary production in the historical formation of Muslim religious culture. Their principal difference concerns how the relationship between Islamic textual authority and indigenous cultural forms should be interpreted. Roy foregrounds cultural mediation and syncretistic formation, while Irani emphasises translation, theological articulation, and the vernacularisation of Islamic salvation history.

Regarding the influence of non-Islamic traditions on Sufism, other scholars, in addition to Roy, Eaton, Stewart, and Irani, have argued that it gradually incorporated Tantric, Yogic, Nātha, and other indigenous practices as it developed in the Indian subcontinent.

Muhammad Enamul Haq (1975), in his A History of Sufi-ism in Bengal, for example, suggests that although the fundamental principles of Sufism in Bengal remained comparable to those of northern India until the sixteenth century, Bengali Sufism subsequently developed closer associations with Tantrikism, Yogism, Nāthism, and other similar systems of indigenous thought and asceticism (p. 52). He identifies conceptual parallels between Sufi understandings of the soul, spiritual discipline, and stages of mystical realisation and corresponding ideas in Hindu and Buddhist traditions. His discussion includes comparisons between the Sufi concepts of rūḥ and al-nafs and the Indic concepts of ātman and citta, as well as between Sufi stages of spiritual realisation and Buddhist accounts of spiritual attainment. Such comparisons draw attention to the intellectual encounters that took place between religious communities in the subcontinent. Nevertheless, in assessing the contributions of Sufis in Bengal, Haq acknowledges that Sufis exerted considerable influence on Vaishnavism, particularly on its concept of prema, or divine love, and that the Vaishnava emphasis on a casteless society appeared to derive from Sufi influence. He maintains, “Growth of cordiality and unity between the Hindus and the Muslims of Bengal is one of the great achievements that the Sufis accomplished in this country” (p. 287).

Abdul Karim (1985) also emphasises the institutional and popular dimensions of Sufism in Bengal. He argues that Muslim rulers, in collaboration with Sufi figures, established mosques, madrasas, and khanqahs, which helped introduce local populations to Islamic teachings and institutions. At the popular level, the authority of pirs and the veneration of their dargahs became central features of Bengali Muslim religious life. Karim associates the popular understanding of pir authority with certain familiar aspects of Hindu and Buddhist religious traditions, including the veneration of spiritual teachers and sacred sites. He suggests that such parallels may have facilitated the acceptance of Sufi figures among populations previously familiar with the authority of Tantric gurus and other religious intermediaries. He observes that the Sufis deeply influenced the masses and that, even at the time of his writing, their dargahs or tombs continued to be visited and venerated by both Muslims and Hindus (p. 160).

These interpretations point to an important distinction between formal Islamic institutions and popular devotional practices. The former provided mechanisms for transmitting scriptural knowledge and normative religious teachings, while the latter offered forms of spiritual guidance, intercession, healing, protection, and communal belonging. This relationship became increasingly contested in subsequent periods.

The accommodationist and locally embedded character of Bengali Muslim religious culture encountered sustained criticism during the nineteenth century. Reformist movements sought to redefine Muslim religious identity by challenging practices they considered incompatible with Islamic scriptural norms. Among the most influential were the Fara'idi movement, the Tariqa-i Muhammadiyya, and the Tayyuni movement.

However, the Fara'idi movement cannot be understood exclusively as a campaign for religious purification, even during the leadership of Haji Shariatullah (d. 1840). Under the leadership of his son Dudu Miyan, it developed into a broader peasant mobilisation against oppressive landlordism and colonial agrarian arrangements. Its appeal among the Muslim peasantry was connected with the social and economic conditions of rural Bengal, particularly the unequal distribution of land and the burdens associated with existing systems of rent and taxation.

The Tariqa-i Muhammadiyya and Tayyuni movements also contributed to debates about Islamic orthodoxy and religious practice. Although they differed in their doctrinal positions, political orientations, and attitudes towards congregational worship, they shared criticisms of certain popular devotional practices. Their disagreements also concerned the legal and political status of British-ruled India and the obligations of Muslims living under non-Muslim political authority (Muinuddin Ahmed Khan, History of the Fara’idi Movement in Bengal (1818–1906), 1965, pp. 89–103).

The reformist criticism of shrine-centred practices should therefore be situated within a broader transformation of Muslim religious authority. These movements sought to privilege scriptural interpretation, obligatory religious observance, and reformist scholarship over certain established forms of popular devotional authority. Their criticism did not necessarily eliminate Sufi institutions, but it changed the terms through which shrine veneration and saintly authority were publicly contested.

Rafiuddin Ahmed (1981, p. 106) characterises an important aspect of nineteenth-century Islamic reform in Bengal as an attempt to reject elements of Bengali cultural life that reformers regarded as incompatible with Islam. This observation highlights the tension between locally rooted religious practices and movements seeking to establish more standardised forms of Islamic identity.

The subsequent expansion of Deobandi-oriented institutions of Islamic learning, colonial education, and other reformist organisations further transformed the religious landscape. In the twentieth century, Tablighi Jama'at and other reform-oriented movements contributed to the continuing debate over the legitimacy of popular Sufi practices. In contemporary Bangladesh, these debates are also reflected in the positions of various Islamist and Salafi-oriented groups, including Jamaat-e-Islami and other religious organisations.

In conclusion, we may say that the history of Sufism in the Bengal delta demonstrates that the Islamisation of the region was neither a singular historical event nor a straightforward process of religious conversion. It involved the transformation of landscapes, the expansion of agricultural settlements, the establishment of religious institutions, the development of devotional practices, and the production of vernacular Islamic knowledge. The persistence of shrine-centred religious life alongside reformist challenges demonstrates that the history of Bengali Islam is not merely a history of conversion but also a history of the continuous negotiation of religious identity, authority, and belonging.
